title: Playing the melody straight before improvising
summary: Edison always plays the melody first, calling it the hardest thing to do.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: As I was saying to George this morning at breakfast, I think it's a good idea the way you very often play the melody in that first chorus before you take off with it.
I mean, it makes sense, doesn't it.
Oh, I always play the melody. Almost note for note before --
Then they know where you're at.

Sure. Then the people -- you establish what you're trying to do to the people, you know. And then after you play the melody, then you start improvising on your melody, then people know that you're a pro then because they know that you're taking that melody and you're weaving your own

ideas around that same note that's so pretty, the melody that the man wrote for you to follow, you know. Like Benny Carter, he wrote -- whoever composed a song, they expend a lot of hours and concentration to write this melody. So that's the guideline you're supposed to follow when you play it, you know. And that's one of the hardest things for a person to do, is play a straight melody. That's one of the hardest, hardest things any musician can do.
And to phrase it real true.

Just play it straight. Not deviate one note from any note. Just to play the straight melody, you know. And I think you can really originate a lot of little things you can play around a melody, you know. I think that's where originality comes from, you know. Originating something around a melody and not taking a melody and just turn it around where people don't know what you're doing, you know. As I said before, I'd much rather be mediocre originator than to be a fantastic imitator.
